transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, well, what brought me in is that I keep leaving my station at work. Or, you know, I'll just keep popping up during meetings when I'm really supposed to stay put. My supervisor told me I had to get it checked out because it's actually becoming a safety problem on the floor. I just... I kind of take off before I even think about it.
Has this difficulty with staying in one place been something you've dealt with since you were a child, or is this something that's started more recently?

It's been since I was a kid. Um, even back in elementary school, I was always the kid who just couldn't stay in my seat. I'd talk over the teacher a lot, and my parents were always getting notes sent home because I kept blurting things out or, you know, just wandering around the room. So yeah, it's definitely not a new thing at all.

When you're working on a task that requires concentration, like reading instructions or completing paperwork, do you find it hard to keep your attention on it, or do you find it easier to focus when you're sitting still?

It's definitely hard to keep my attention on it. Sitting still doesn't really make it any easier, honestly. Like, when I have to do inventory logs or read through the CNC training pages at work, I start out really trying. But after just a few minutes, the numbers or the words just start to blur together. I end up having to keep going back and reading the same thing over again because I realize I didn't actually take any of it in.
Besides work, do you notice these same problems with staying focused and sitting still in other parts of your life — like at home or when you're doing things socially?

Yeah, I mean, it definitely happens at home and when I'm hanging out with people, too. But honestly, it's work where it's really messing up my life right now. 

It's actually put my job and my certification plans at serious risk. My supervisors have already written me up for safety and production problems because I keep wandering off or losing track of what I'm doing. And... it's getting bad with the other people on the floor, too. My coworkers are getting frustrated, and they're a lot less willing to partner with me during handoffs now because they know I'm not focused.

When you do manage to sit down and focus, or even just in everyday situations, do you find yourself getting frustrated or irritable pretty quickly? Or do you ever act on impulses without thinking about the consequences?

I don't really know if I get frustrated or irritable that easily, honestly. I mean, I don't think so? And as for acting on impulses... I'm not really sure what you mean by that, or if I do that. I just mostly struggle with the not being able to stay still and focus part.

When you're sitting down—say, at a desk or in a meeting—do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, like tapping your fingers or bouncing your leg, or do you feel this physical restlessness that makes it hard to keep still?

Yeah, definitely. If I have to sit for, like, the certification class or a safety meeting at work, my foot is always bouncing. I'll be clicking a pen, or... picking at my sleeves. I just end up shifting around in my seat so much that people actually ask me to stop. It's just really hard to just stay still.
When you think back to elementary school, do you remember these problems with sitting still, focusing, and fidgeting starting before you were about 12 years old, or did they begin later than that?

Yeah, it definitely started way before I was 12. Even back in elementary school, I was always the kid who couldn't stay in my seat. I remember I would talk over the teacher a lot, and my parents were always getting notes sent home because I kept blurting things out or just wandering around the classroom when we were supposed to be working. So, yeah, it's been going on for a really long time.

You mentioned that the focus and restlessness problems are really affecting your job right now. Besides work, are these issues also causing problems in other parts of your life — like making it harder to manage things at home, or affecting your relationships with friends or family?

I don't really notice it as much at home or with my friends, to be honest. It's mostly just work that I'm really worried about right now. 

It's gotten so bad that it's actually putting my job and my certification plans at risk. My supervisors have already written me up for safety and production problems. And... well, my coworkers are getting a lot less willing to partner with me during handoffs because of it. So that's the main place it's really messing things up for me.

I hear you that work is where you're noticing the biggest problems right now. But when you think about managing things at home — like keeping up with chores, paying bills on time, or organizing your space — do you find yourself struggling with focus or follow-through there as well?

Um, no, not really. I don't really have a problem with that stuff. I mean, I pay my bills and do my chores fine. My place isn't perfectly organized or anything, but it's not an issue. Like I said, it's really just at work where I'm struggling to keep things together.

When you're driving or doing other activities where you need to pay attention to stay safe, do you ever find yourself zoning out or missing things, or do you feel like you have to work really hard to keep your mind on what you're doing?

No, I don't really have any problems when I'm driving. I mean, I pay attention fine and I've never gotten into an accident or anything because I zoned out. It's really just at work where I can't seem to focus on what I'm supposed to be doing.

You mentioned that the focus and restlessness problems are mainly happening at work. When you're doing things you find interesting or enjoyable — like hobbies, activities you like, or things that really capture your attention — do you still have trouble focusing and sitting still, or does that get easier?

No, if it's something I actually like doing, I don't have those problems. I can focus on it just fine, and I don't feel like I have to keep moving around or anything. It's way easier. Like I keep saying, it's really just at work where everything is going wrong for me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that began in elementary school (before age 12) and has persisted into adulthood. Core ADHD symptoms are clearly present: difficulty sustaining attention on non-preferred tasks, excessive fidgeting and restlessness, and impulsive behavior (leaving workstation without forethought). However, the symptoms show marked situation-specificity: they are prominent at work but notably absent or minimal in other life domains (home, driving, hobbies, relationships). This context-dependent presentation, combined with the patient's ability to focus well on preferred activities and the absence of significant functional impairment outside the work setting, suggests the diagnosis is ADHD, Combined Presentation (F90.2) cannot be fully supported. The predominant presentation appears to be Predominantly Inattentive Type (F90.1) given the emphasis on attention difficulties, though hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms are also present. Given the atypical pattern of situation-specificity and the lack of clear pervasive functional impairment across multiple life domains as typically required for ADHD diagnosis, F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) is selected as the most accurate code, with F90.1 and F91.9 as differential considerations.
